"Toward Interactive Green Urban Planning: Assessing the Efficiency of Urban Green Spaces and Integrating Low-Cost Smart System Solutions"
items.samenvatting_bron: Abstract: This study presents a comparative field diagnosis of urban green spaces in the city of Annaba (Algeria), focusing on Edough Sud Garden (central sample) and Martyr Zemmouri Uenassa Garden (neighborhood sample). The research aims to assess the condition of vegetation, facilities, maintenance levels, and waste management, while exploring the integration of low-cost smart solutions—such as soil-moisture sensors for irrigation, fill-level waste sensors, and interactive QR code platforms—to enhance sustainable urban management.

items.titel: Understanding public preferences for urban wildflower meadows
items.samenvatting_bron: Accelerating urbanisation challenges biodiversity and human wellbeing, demanding effective urban nature-based solutions. Urban wildflower meadows are increasingly popular interventions that may offer biodiversity and wellbeing benefits. However, realising their potential depends on public support, which requires robust evidence on which meadow design attributes the public prefers and values most. We conducted a choice experiment with urban greenspace users across three UK cities to quantify willingness-to-pay (WTP) for some of the key characteristics of wildflower meadows in public parks, namely flower colour diversity, native species composition, plant species richness, and pollinator habitat quality. Respondents generally preferred wildflower meadow options over the status quo of mown amenity grass and were willing to pay for improvements to meadow attributes through increased local taxation. Respondents had positive WTP for more colourful, pollinator-friendly meadows with more native species, but not for additional plant species. Preferences were largely consistent across respondents interviewed at different meadow types (annual, perennial, or control sites), suggesting that enhanced attribute salience from direct exposure to existing meadows had minimal influence on stated preferences. Methodologically, this suggests that in situ surveys of preferences for urban greenspace are broadly robust to salience effects and can inform management beyond the surveyed sites. Attribut
